newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: EU commissioner opposes huge subsidies for East.
newsitem.headline: EU commissioner opposes huge subsidies for East.

text.p: The European Union's budget commissioner spoke out on Tuesday against showering new members from post-communist Europe with subsidies, saying this would distort their economies and breed a dependency culture.

Commissioner Erkki Liikanen said that the EU's structural funds, which help countries modernise their industrial economies, and the common agricultural policy (CAP) could not be applied in their present forms to new members from the East.
Together the CAP and structural funds account for 80 percent of EU spending among the existing 15 members, he told a conference in the Czech capital of Prague.
Referring to structural funds, he said: "Most if not all candidate countries would under present arrangements be eligible immediately upon accession for improbable sums."
The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are tipped to become the first former East Bloc countries to join the EU some time early in the next millenium.

Under present rules the Czechs would qualify for huge structural funds to modernise their communist-era industrial areas while the Poles and Hungarians could expect big agricultural subsidies. The cost of this would be huge.

"Unless other areas of the (EU) budget were to be cut to the bone, which is not an option, member states will not be prepared to countenance such an increase in structural fund spending," said Liikanen.

"A straightforward application of the existing policy in the candidate countries would be counterproductive for the applicant countries themselves," he told a conference organised by the Czech business-backed Bohemiae Foundation.
Member states have to match EU structural funds under co-financing arrangements, which would put a heavy burden on the tight national budgets of most post-communist countries.
The sums could also be huge in proportion to the gross domestic product (GDP) of the former East Bloc countries, which remain poor by Western European standards.

"If the community budget gave, in various forms, in the order of 10 to 15 or even 20-25 percent of candidates' GDP, a dependency culture would result," said Liikanen. "This could remove normal incentives to development."

He also said that the CAP had to be further reformed before negotiations even began with applicants from the East. Income support for farmers, a plank of the CAP, would give a big rise in living standards for central and eastern European farmers.
But this could distort economies of the post-communist countries, which are trying to modernise their industries and build up service sectors which scarely existed under communism.
"Capital would be transferred from industry and services to agriculture, and land prices would saw and that is not the intention of enlargement for any of the candidates," he said.
